analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from selling or profiting from your faceprints, fingerprints, and voiceprints without consent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2020 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company collecting biometric identifiers — retina scans, faceprints, voiceprints, fingerprints — to get your written consent first, tell you exactly what they were collecting and why, delete the data within a set time, and keep it as secure as other sensitive information. It would have banned selling, leasing, or otherwise profiting from that data, and let individuals sue companies that violated the rules, with $1,000 in damages per negligent violation. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday consumers and employees whose faces, fingerprints, and voiceprints are scanned by apps, phones, workplaces, and stores. They gain the right to know what biometric data a company holds, to refuse collection, to have it destroyed on schedule, and to sue if a company profits from it or leaks it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and employees scanned by apps and employers

how_it_helps.text: Companies could not collect a biometric identifier without first telling the person in writing what is being collected, the purpose, and the time term, and getting a written release [S3].
Companies in possession of biometric data were barred from selling, leasing, trading, using it for advertising, or otherwise profiting from it [S3].

Companies had to publish a retention policy and permanently destroy biometric data by the earlier of when the original purpose is satisfied or one year after the person's last interaction, unless a court warrant or subpoena applied [S3].
Individuals got a right to know: on request, a business had to disclose free of charge what biometric data it collected about them over the previous 12 months [S3].

Anyone harmed by a violation could sue for at least $1,000 per negligent violation or actual damages, plus attorneys' fees, and for punitive damages up to $5,000 per violation for intentional or reckless violations; state attorneys general could also sue on residents' behalf [S3].
Information obtained in violation of the bill could not be used by the federal government in criminal or civil proceedings, except in cases alleging a violation of the bill itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect or monetize biometric data — facial recognition vendors, adtech and data brokers, and any business scanning faces or fingerprints — would bear compliance costs, face destruction deadlines, lose the ability to sell the data, and face class-action litigation exposure. Some costs could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, adtech, and biometric-scanning businesses

drawbacks.text: The private right of action with $1,000 in statutory damages per violation invites large class-action suits over technical violations — a pattern seen under the similar Illinois biometric law — which can be costly even for small businesses that caused no actual harm [S3].

Compliance requires written consent systems, published retention policies, and destruction infrastructure, a real cost for small businesses that use fingerprint time clocks or face-unlock systems, though the bill allows an employment release executed as a condition of employment [S3].

The bill excludes federal, state, and local government agencies and their contractors from its definitions, so the largest biometric databases — government-run law enforcement face and fingerprint collections — are left untouched by its consent and sale rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are strong and targeted: consent before collection, no profiting from biometric data, mandatory deletion, and a right to sue. The main honest costs are compliance burdens and litigation exposure that fall hardest on smaller businesses, and the carve-out for government agencies means the bill regulates the private market while leaving public-sector biometric surveillance alone. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the costs, though the per-violation damages formula could use calibration.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley, joined by Sen. Bernie Sanders, introduced the bill on August 3, 2020 [S3, S4].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1, S5].
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect and monetize biometric data — facial recognition vendors, data brokers, and adtech — are better off, because no federal rule now requires consent, limits profiting, or mandates deletion of faceprints and fingerprints. Consumers remain in the same position as before, protected only by a patchwork of state laws the bill explicitly would not have preempted [S3].

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Lindsey Graham)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat unreferred no further than committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the record shows only two sponsors (one Democrat, one Independent) and no recorded opposition or support from other senators.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance vendors
industries.note: These firms' business is scanning and matching faces, fingerprints, and voices. The bill would require consent before collection and bar profiting from the data, cutting off their core revenue streams. Their gain from the bill's death is the public's continued lack of federal protection over their own biometric identifiers.

The bill flatly prohibited selling, leasing, trading, or using biometric data for advertising. These firms profit by trading exactly this data, so their interest runs directly against the consumers whose faces and voices are the commodity.

The bill allows collection with informed written consent for a valid service purpose, so phones and apps using face or fingerprint unlock could continue operating. But they would face consent, deletion, and security obligations they do not currently have under federal law.

industries.industry: Employers using biometric time clocks and workplace scanning
industries.note: The bill permits a release executed as a condition of employment, so fingerprint timekeeping could continue. But employers would owe employees disclosure, deletion deadlines, and damages for violations — protections employees currently lack in most states.
